utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon. I'll be very brief. I wanted to raise one quick matter, reflected in the Trial Chamber's decision of the 29th of September regarding the materials seized from the Bukanjac [phoen] premises, including the DVDs and the hard-drive materials. As the OTP indicated in its submission of the 20th of September, the review and indexing of the hard-drive materials, in contrast to the DVD materials, has been ongoing due to the circumstances referred to in the confidential annex. The bulk of those materials will be disclosed early next week, and the remainder of the materials the week following. I simply raise that because we noted that the Trial Chamber's decision appeared to reflect a misapprehension that the hard-drive materials, in addition to the DVD materials, were disclosed on the 31st of August, and I wanted to clarify that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, that was also my misapprehension. I'm hearing for the first time today that there are undisclosed materials from that January 2010 -- or December 2009 search, and that may cause us to seek another suspension of the proceedings if a first glance of that undisclosed material indicates that it's anything like the material that has been disclosed to us. So I also want to put that on record at this point, and we'll simply await the material to see what has to be done next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I may, Mr. President, and no point in any extended discussion or argument now, but the submission makes clear, as I noted, what the status was with respect to the hard-drive materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your submission is well noted. We'll see what we need to do. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, let's continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. Do you agree with me that UNPROFOR faced a lot of difficulty due to the undefined status of the protected area, the fact that the demilitarisation process was not resolved, and, generally speaking, with the situation in which they didn't know how to treat such zones?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly difficulties with the lack of definition of the boundaries and the fact that one of the parties to the conflict had not demilitarised the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it would be the Muslim side, of course, that had its troops in the zones; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we discussed that previously, and the status was different for the Bosnian Government side than it was for the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we refuse to accept that, General. Before the conflict and during the conflict, we fought and finally achieved an equal status. Who was it who suggested to you that we should be treated as rebels or, in other words, in any way different than the Muslim government?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian nation was a recognised member of the United Nations. The Republika Srpska had not yet been recognised by any entity at all, other than the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, General, Caligula proclaimed his horse as senator, but he wasn't a senator. Over 70 per cent of the territory was in our hands. What did we care that nobody recognised us? We were part of that Bosnia, one of the three sides, and you treated us as rebels. I don't mean you, personally, but a large majority of the international community treated us as rebels, as an illegal entity, and that's why we're all here today. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, the United Nations Protection Force were acting as mediators in a conflict which they were trying to bring to an end through peaceful means, and their approach to the three warring parties was impartial, although, of course, they didn't remain neutral in terms of the final outcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D291 is the next document I would like to call, and you will see how the Serbs and Croats perceived that matter at the time. And I'm talking about a majority of the population, the Christian part of the population composed of Croats and Serbs who made up over 50 per cent, and well over the 70 per cent of the territory belonged to those two peoples. And according to the International Pact on Human Rights, the resources in a territory belong to the people who resided in the territory. Here, General, Kresimir Zubak and Nikola Koljevic on the 10th of February, 1994, immediately after your arrival -- please look at bullet point 6. That's the only one. They achieved an agreement on the nature of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina: [In English] "An absolute majority of the population on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina opt for peace and ask the Muslim people to agree with this decision." [Interpretation] Therefore, it would be much easier for all of us -- it would have been easier if the international community had treated us as one of the three sides and not as rebels, and the OTP has incriminated even the setting up of our parties. Can this be admitted, Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general has already answered the question and said that we were treated as three equal sides, and you can see here that all the three equal sides, the Serbs and the Croats, constituted a majority. Look at bullet point 3: [In English] "The so-called Presidency and Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina do not represent --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is not a forum for you to make a speech. Ask a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you know that the Presidency of Yugoslavia that was left by Croats and Serbs was often referred to as a rump presidency?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, if that is correct, by the analogy, would the Muslim Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina also be rightly called a rump presidency? Look at bullet point 3, where the Croatian and Serbian representatives denied the Presidency the right to represent the Croatian and Serbian people. It is not even a rump presidency; it is just a presidency constituted of the representatives of only one ethnic group. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've explained, Dr. Karadzic, as an officer of the United Nations, I could only work within the rules that had been laid down by the United Nations for that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not attacking you. I'm just asking you to either agree with me or deny the fact that there were three equal sides and that the three sides constituted Bosnia. Is that correct, those were three equal sides? It was not like they were Bosnia and the rest of us were rebels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered that question. I will tell you to move on to your next question. Ms. Edgerton, do you object to the admission of this document? I'm not sure whether this is signed or not, Mr. Karadzic, before it is to be admitted at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, there was an agreement about that document. However, Mr. Tudjman did not want the document to be signed. There may even be a signed version, but Tudjman asked for the document not to be publicised; therefore, not to be signed. He just wanted the Muslims to be orally informed about its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we know absolutely nothing about this document and the provenance, its authenticity. I'd object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll wait for another witness to admit this. So we'll not admit this at this time, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we then call 65 ter 10689.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in view of the fact that you didn't know -- or, rather, you did not have the boundaries for the protected zones, you didn't have the agreement on the contents of the Gorazde zone, would you perhaps agree with me that there was no legal grounds to call for NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with you. The United Nations Security Council resolution was quite plain, that is, 824 and 836, that the United Nations should use all means possible to deter attacks against the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, if you didn't know what the enclave was, how did you know that it came under attack? You didn't have boundaries. The zone was not demilitarised. How were you able to know when the boundaries of the enclave were over-stepped if there were no boundaries at all, to speak of?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was self-evident when the civilian populations in these enclaves came into danger, either from the point of view of their own lives or their property. That was the moment at which the United Nations decided to take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the side that had brought the civilians in danger should be bombed? Yes or no. And then later we will show who it was who actually brought them into a dangerous position.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, those who were shelling the civilian populations were liable -- in those enclaves were liable to have action taken against them under the United Nations Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you exerted a certain caution because the NATO commands, and especially Admiral Smith and Admiral Burda, were prone to be trigger-happy, as it were, and that you tried hard to avert the NATO actions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw the use of NATO air-strikes as a measure of last resort. We did not see ourselves as part of the conflict between the warring parties. And as long as the conflict was not endangering the lives or the property of the civilians within the safe areas, then we took no action, other than to report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not complaining against the United Nations. Were the United Nations afraid of the over-zealousness of NATO commanders to open fire on Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a continual debate between the United Nations and NATO about the level of force to be used, and the United Nations never changed their position that they could not embark on war-fighting levels of force. They had to restrict themselves to those that were compatible with a peacekeeping mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are avoiding to tell me what the NATO position was, but we'll come to that with the help of documents. Look at this document. Is this a telegram sent by your assistant for Civilian Affairs, Viktor Andreev, to Ambassador Akashi? And the date of the document is 14 April 1994 -- or, rather, the 18th of April. I apologise. That was in the middle of the crisis, eight days after the bombardment. Could you please say your answer for the record?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a telegram, dated 18 April, sent by Andreev to Akashi?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is. I can't see, incidentally, the bottom of that document, but I recognise the top half of it, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page. We can't see the whole document at a time, although we would like to draw everybody's attention to the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at bullet point 10, first of all: [In English] "The council must clarify the concept of the safe area --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, we could actually have the document made just a little bit smaller so we could all see the whole document on one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought he was referring to three pages. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does have three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to paragraph 10: [In English] "The council must clarify the concept of the safe areas as soon as possible. Until now, they have never been geographically defined, and it has never been clear how UNPROFOR was meant to deter attacks on them, or whether, indeed, UNPROFOR should have tolerated their use by the Bosnian Army for military purposes. If the council decided to continue with the concept, it must be willing to give the resources and the political commitment necessary to do so. Otherwise, we invite conflict with the Serbs for the benefit -- for no benefit to anyone." [Interpretation] So the 10th of April bombing had to happen in order for this telegram to be sent. It says here, We don't know what a protected zone is, and if this continues, we will have a conflict with the Serbs on our hands; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must understand, Dr. Karadzic, that the United Nations and NATO were moving into new territory when it came to the employment of NATO air-strikes on a peacekeeping mission. This had never happened before, and the United Nations Security Council resolutions that were passed reflect very much the ongoing debate about what the levels of force should be used in a peacekeeping mission. On the ground, we were quite clear that they could not go beyond what we deemed to be appropriate to a peacekeeping mission, and that was the minimum use of force to achieve a specific aim, whether that be to deter attacks against a safe area, or to enforce the passage of a convoy, or to defend the lives and property of the UN peacekeepers, themselves. What you're seeing in this telegram is an element to debate as the two organisations were moving into new territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Objection, General. Was an additional purpose of the attack, and that was to save the army from defeat? After having attacked us, when we engaged in a counter-attack, you came in -- or, rather, NATO came in to save it. But look at bullet point eight, please: [In English] "The question of air power must be treated with the utmost gravity. As the Serbs showed this week, they are prepared to run the risk of escalation. If the international community is not similarly committed, it should realise that limited close air support will engage the Serbs, provoking a back-lash against the UN personnel on the ground."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, that was one of the possibilities that had to be considered, particularly as our main job was to deliver humanitarian aid to the people who needed it, some 2.7 million people in Bosnia at that time, including 600.000 Serbs. And had the Serb side, who, as we've already explained, dominated most of the territory and, therefore, most of the routes used for the delivery of humanitarian aid, blocked all those with military force, there was little that the United Nations, as peacekeepers, could do to deliver that aid. Therefore, the use of force and the levels of the use of force were under continual scrutiny and debate, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, bullet point 10 shows that there are no grounds to aid the BiH army, because that would, indeed, have been aid administered to the army and a signal to the BH Army to abuse the protected zone. But when you're talking about the blockade of roads, let's look at the following page and see what the cause is and what the consequences were. Let's see whether the Serbs deserved to be attacked because they had blocked the roads, or was it the other way around? Did perhaps the Serbs block the roads because of the attack? Let's look at bullet point 11: [In English] "... the Serbs --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you read the English part again? If you change your language from Serbian to English, you need to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I see. Point 11: "UNPROFOR's mandate has pushed it into low-level conflict with the Serbs. As a result, Sarajevo --" I repeat: "As a result, Sarajevo is blockaded, its airport is closed, food stocks are declining. Our mandate must either be one within which we are able to have a co-operative relationship with the Serbs, or it must be one in which we have the force to impose our will. It cannot be, as it is now, somewhere in between."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like us to determine whether the Serbs were evil and that's why blocked the roads with no reason at all, or whether the blocking of the roads and the harsh letter by General Milovanovic were all provoked by something. Were we provoked into acting the way we did or did we do all those things out of the blue? Bullet point 11 shows that the cause was pushing UNPROFOR into a low intensity conflict with the Serbs, and the consequence was the intensification of the situation and the tensions with the Serbs. And if we add to that, General, that we had a reason to doubt the sincerity of the lower levels of command and that they were smuggling weapons and fuel to the Muslims, then you can obviously see why we thought that the United Nations were working to our detriment.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the NATO bombing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse -- please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the NATO bombing, the blocking of the routes by the Serb side was both systematic and frequent, but not complete. After the bombing and air-strikes took place, for a period of time the blocking of the roads was 100 per cent throughout the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the last question of yours was rather a statement. In the future, I may cut off you in the middle. Just refrain from making a speech. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D687, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the Court please produce D143, just to show you, General, the reasons that existed before the bombing for controls and blockades. The document number is D143. Please do not think that I am attacking either you, or the United Nations, or Great Britain, or any of the higher commands. However, this doesn't change the fact that we had good reasons, and you will see them in the document. And we're waiting for the document to be displayed on the screen. Here you have it. "Movement by convoys, teams and individuals from UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations." Everybody please look at how convoys moved and how many convoys there were, and how were checks and controls carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is there a date to this document so that we can have it in some measure of context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an overview for the year 1994. In the document, we will see this is an overview for the year 1994, segregated by month. In paragraph 1, it says in the course of 1994, convoys passed every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, for seven or eight months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we see page 5. Page 5. It says it's a table reflecting the year of 1994. Is it fine, Ms. Edgerton, now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the question of the timing, yes. I have no idea what the source of the document is, though, by who it might have been generated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see. Let's carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the first page, and let's look how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one corps, the Drina Corps, is sending its report in the first part, and they are reporting about the movement of humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR across its territory. And it says in the first paragraph: "They moved about on a daily basis during 1994 using the following roads:" And then the following passage: "The entry and exit of convoys was controlled at seven check-points ..." And those check-points are then listed. And then: "Entry controls and inspection of persons, weapons, vehicles, loads and documentation are conducted at check-points by members of the civilian police and by teams generally made up of personnel who have been working at this task since August 1993 ...," and so on and so forth. "... who have attained sufficient experience ..." And so on and so forth. Can we go on to the following page. Bullet point C, I believe you will see it: "Behaviour and abuse of mandate by UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations." Here you have it. Let's go to the third paragraph immediately: "In 1994, as previously, checks mostly revealed the following attempts at abuse: "Transport of goods which are not permitted at all in UNPROFOR convoys; "Transport of goods which do not constitute humanitarian aid - in convoys of humanitarian organisations; "Transport of goods in quantities greater than those permitted." And then the last paragraph on the same page: "Understandably, most cases of attempted smuggling of goods were in the convoys for Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde, which had the least opportunity to obtain goods outside of humanitarian goods. The following goods were mostly smuggled: Video cameras, photographic cameras, films, weapons, radio sets, satellite equipment --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the following page. It starts with: "Understandably, in most cases ..." And that's on the top of that page, "smuggling" -- or "smuggled," actually. We can see what things were smuggled: antennas, signal devices, optical devices, night vision apparatus, Motorolas, various parts for devices, antifreeze, chemical manure, oxygen cylinders, flak-jackets, helmets, sleeping bags, military apparel and -- can we have the following page in the Serbian language -- and different food stuffs. Yes, that's it. I'll skip one part: "There's no doubt that there would have been very few attempts to smuggle non-permitted goods if these had been confiscated permanently at the check-points, because temporary confiscation merely enforces delay and leaves the actors the hope that they will succeed in getting them to their destination at the next attempt ...." Which means that the goods were temporarily seized, and when the convoy returned, they were returned to them: "When representatives of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations complained about the procedure of the organs at the check-points --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now that we've read that paragraph, come to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, despite the fact that you brought a lot of peace to the theatre of war, and especially in Sarajevo, you pacified it, would you agree that those were the reasons why Serbs had to be cautious with regard to the convoys? And since we were three times under-powered, there was an imminent danger that we would finally be defeated because our enemy was helped in this particular way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I would absolutely deny that the United Nations facilitated or, indeed, took part in the smuggling of any weapons or other military equipment to the other side. Secondly, all three parties to the conflict had signed, when the United Nations Protection Force first deployed into Bosnia, an agreement that there would be free movement of all convoys. The performance on the ground by the three warring parties fell far short of that, particularly the blocking of convoys by the Serb side. For example, in February 1994, looking at the World Health Organisation figures, less than 50 per cent of goods were delivered to the people who needed it, and, of course, without that, they were suffering greatly, without that aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, how could the Muslims block that when Serbs and Croats were around them? They could have only got all of that from the territory held by Serbs and Croats. That is why you proportionately had more problems with the Serbs, because it was only through Serb-held territory that you could have supplied humanitarian aid to the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that because the Serbs controlled 70 per cent of the territory of the country in 1994, it was inevitable that most of the routes for the delivery of humanitarian aid ran through territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb side. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. You see what my point is, General. This shows that the Serbs had reason to thoroughly check the convoys because there was the danger of their defeat, because in some convoys -- I mean, I'm not accusing the UN or command, but from somewhere goods were smuggled that presented a danger to us, and they were a danger to us. Was this done only because Serbs were evil, as such, or were they afraid of being defeated?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say -- I have no idea what the motivation may have been, but all I can say is that the majority of the blocking of the convoys, for the reasons we've already discussed, came from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, whether you can remember the degree of that control over a convoy varied, depending upon the content of it, i.e., whether it's an UNPROFOR convoy or it was a humanitarian convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, most of the convoys through the Serb side were escorted by the UNPROFOR. There were two parts to the mission. UNHCR provided the lorries, the drivers, and the goods, in terms of humanitarian aid, and the United Nations Protection Force escorted them where it was decided that escorts were required. On some occasions, they ran without escorts. On other occasions, they needed the UN to help them move their convoys, both from the point of view of control and also to deter any blocking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second category of convoy, of course, was the military convoys which UNPROFOR ran in order to supply their own forces in the enclaves, and, of course, Sarajevo was an enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if it was a military convoy, a different rule must have been applied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clearly, we didn't have participation from UNHCR on those convoys; we merely ran them ourselves. But they were equally subject to the inspection and control procedures by the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document has already been admitted, so now we're going to ask for 1D1692.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree, don't you, General, that you, yourself, said in your book that the Serbs took their time as they were conducting the checks, but the flow of humanitarian aid went on, and the interruptions were never such that they required NATO intervention. There is a sentence to that effect in your book; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'd have to remind me as to what that sentence was. But it is certainly the case that the UN managed to maintain a level of flow of humanitarian aid throughout the war, in spite of all the difficulties that were placed in front of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have we got the document? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, "Activities of UNPROFOR," that's what it says down here. Do we have a translation? No, we do not have a translation: "3. Situation in the territory. "A. Activities of UNPROFOR." And then the first bullet point says: "Military observers," and then the second one: "Convoy Premijer-Urgence passed through the airport from Igman towards Sarajevo. They were taken to the check-point Ilidza, and according to the first information we received, in addition to food, they transported ammunition as well. Details are being checked." Do you remember that that happened several times at the airport, that goods were found of this nature that were being sent to our enemies?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 10 down there: "From the check-point MC Betanija, UNPROFOR withdrew their forces for reasons unknown." And then it says: "Around 2030 hours on the 8th of April, a humanitarian aid convoy was checked that was being sent to the city of Sarajevo, seven trucks and one jeep. A large quantity of ammunition for a Browning and sanitary material was found, and that was not on the list of goods that were being transported. All of the vehicles were seized, and the goods were stored at the warehouse of the Ilidza Brigade, and the persons involved, drivers and escorts, were sent to the Command of the SRK for further examination." This is a regular report for the 8th of April, and it shows clearly that ammunition was found for a Browning that would have killed our soldiers. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no knowledge of any such incident taking place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, our PR people didn't manage to get this through to the media. However, this is a regular report. So can it be admitted? And let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only on the basis of its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The authenticity of this document is not disputed, and it covers the issue which is relevant to one of the topics the witness has dealt with. So on that basis, we'll admit it. But we'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D688, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P1859 [as interpreted], I'd like to have that document called up now so the general can see it. P859. This is a telegram. Can we see it? No, we cannot. Oh, yes, we can now. P859, fine. That's the 26th of July, 1994, and it says here "Message." [In English] "The Bosnian Serbs have announced that they are denouncing part of the agreement of freedom of movement for the Sarajevo area of 17 March 1994, which will effectively cut off the life-lines route that links Sarajevo to the outside world. The routes affected will be those which cross the airport (Dobrinja-Butmir and Lukeska-Ilidza). The Bratstvo-Jedinstvo Bridge and the route Sarajevo-Visoko (via Vogosca) will remain open." [Interpretation] Later on, it says: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic yesterday wanted to speak to HCR to convey this message to him personally. Finally, I was called and was handed the attached letter. This is the only non-Serb-controlled route between Sarajevo and all other destinations. "The Serbs give four reasons for breaking with the freedom of movement agreement of 17th March: "1. The smuggling of weapons; "2. Sniper activities; "3. Prisoner exchange; and "4. Cease-fire violation." Can we have the second page. The second page is an addendum to the telegram. It's my letter sent to Sergio de Mello and to Viktor Andreev. You see all the things that I say in that letter, and the last sentence reads. "Humanitarian convoys are free to utilize the earlier routes across our territory." [Interpretation] However, these routes where the smuggling had taken place were closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, that this was not done without a reason? Very specific reasons were mentioned, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly remember you raising those issues with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you agree that we only closed those routes where smuggled goods had been seized, and that the other routes remained opened?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree, because I can't know what your motivation was. Our general view was that the Bosnian Serb side were using the closure of routes as a means of levering the Bosnian Government into accepting peace on their terms, and they would use all sorts of reasons for closing these routes, including the ones that you outlined in your letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this letter. It says this very clearly. It's only the routes where we caught the smugglers are being closed: [In English] "Of course humanitarian convoys are free to utilise the earlier routes across our territory." [Interpretation] General, this is not pressure against the Muslim side in order to achieve something, politically speaking, although the international community had imposed sanctions on the Serbs, and that was pressure. However, we did not close all routes. We only closed those routes where there had been smuggling. That is quite clear. The telegram and the letter state that very clearly, that the routes via the airport are being closed, because that's where the smuggling had taken place, whereas the route via Vogosca remained open; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again Dr. Karadzic is arguing with General Rose, which he has been doing since we began this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question, unless you have something to add to that. But please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since this has already been admitted, now I'd like to ask for 9117. That's the 65 ter number of the document I'd like to see now. Let us see what happened in February, what you've been saying. 559117 [as interpreted]. I don't know whether we have a translation. I'm going to tell what this document is. It's the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska writing to the commands of all corps. This is an order of Milovanovic, the chief of staff, and I'm just going to read paragraph 3 to you. You can see the rest: "All check-points should be reinforced with select personnel that will display a higher level of professional kindness, co-operativeness, and simplify procedures involved when examining convoys. Avoid conflict situations and notify the Operative Centre of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska by telephone if any occur."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that the main cause of misunderstandings at check-points were misunderstandings? Either goods appeared that were not on the lists, or persons who were not on the lists, or even extra trucks would appear, two or three extra trucks? Do you remember that that was the main reason why convoys were being detained?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly I remember that there was an undue bureaucratic level that was employed against us, or employed -- more accurately, put -- against the running of the convoys. As I say, all sorts of reasons were employed, including the failure to comply 100 per cent to the checklist or the manifest on a particular vehicle. That is certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, a soldier of yours who receives information to the effect that a convoy is going to appear at his check-point, does he have relative freedom to let something pass that had not been declared or does he have to ask you for extra permission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You, sir, or one of your representatives had already signed a document agreeing to the full and free running of convoys, which, of course, should not have included inspections. But by the time I arrived in 1994, that practice had already started, regrettably, and continued, in spite of efforts to stop it. In theory, those convoys should have run without being stopped or checked at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, General, we never accepted running convoys unchecked. That can only happen in an occupied country. Where you came, with our consent, we had the right to see whether what is contained is what you had declared. If that is not the case and if you are helping our enemies, then it is our right to check that. Would you allow that kind of thing to happen in your own country, to let someone drive something around without any checks?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say, there was an agreement. Because, of course, the populations of all three sides were suffering from the conflict, an agreement had been signed before I arrived in Bosnia; I think in 1992. Certainly I can remember seeing that document, saying that all parties to the conflict agreed to the free running of humanitarian aid convoys. Sadly, that was not to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think that free running of convoys excludes the right to checks?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it should do. But by the time I arrived, as I say, that certainly wasn't the case, and it was impossible, therefore, to go back to the status quo ante, which should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, no one can pass through a war zone without any checks. You know that full well. We had the right to inspect this, and we did so. Look at this sentence: "In depth, we should have forces that can prevent the forceful entry of UNPROFOR." You were there with our consent and with certain regulations involved. You were not an occupying army, and you did not aspire to be one; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The status of the United Nations was that it was a peacekeeping mission, facilitating the humanitarian -- the delivery of humanitarian aid with the consent of the warring parties. That was its status.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the last sentence and let's be done with this document. General Milovanovic is issuing the following order: "All planned and approved convoys should be allowed to cross the territory of Republika Srpska once they are inspected." So he says that it should be done simply, professionally, with appropriate kindness. So all planned and approved convoys. There was a procedure involved once all the goods contained in the said convoys had been inspected. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what was your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is whether the general knows that we had the right to inspection and that our commands had ordered professional, speedy, and proper checks. So there is no doubt that there should have been checks. There should have been checks. So what General Milovanovic is writing here is what the Serbian Army actually did. The general had said that in February we had prevented convoys from passing through, and this is a document from February showing that we were not preventing the convoys from running in any way, but we just wanted to have proper checks and to have them inspected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All repetition. I think the general has answered all those questions. We'll mark for identification this document, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D689, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 13354, 65 ter number. 13354, that's a document -- yes, this is the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document that was in force when you arrived. It had been issued a month prior to your arrival. So this is a document that was issued by the president of the republic. Yours truly, that is. So this is what it says: "With a view to securing normal functioning of humanitarian organisations --" Sorry, let me just say something else before that. It's sent to the Government of Republika Srpska, the Supreme Headquarters of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Health, and the Government Co-ordination Body for Co-operation with UNPROFOR and International Organisations. So this is what the first paragraph says: "With the aim of securing normal functioning of humanitarian organisations, it is necessary that you provide undisturbed passage of all convoys of the humanitarian aid going along the roads and corridors of Republic of Srpska, and which are organised by the UNHCR, the International Committee of the Red Cross, Medecins Sans Frontieres, Handicap-International, the World Health Organisation, the International Committee of Salvation." Were these organisations present, and did you know that we had authorised their presence, as such?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm well aware that those organisations were present in Bosnia, and they were there with the agreement of the warring parties; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a look at the next page of this presidential document. Yes, the second paragraph here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After opinion was obtained, the committee gives its consent for the movement of convoys, and all persons manning check-points have to abide by this, et cetera, et cetera. Do you remember that Professor Koljevic, one of the top officials of Republika Srpska, the vice-president of the republic, headed the committee for humanitarian issues, or, rather, for co-operation with you and humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly remember Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have the second page of this document in English? What we have is only one page. I just noted -- let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure where that part is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "As for checking the contents of the convoy --" that's the second paragraph in Serbian -- "and its vehicles shall be carried out by joint military and police patrols when entering Republika Srpska, and from the point where they're unloaded or where they're crossing the territory or other parts of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, convoys shall be escorted by police patrols. What is prohibited is stopping convoys and re-inspecting them, and especially the unauthorised seizure of goods that had already undergone appropriate procedures." I don't have to read out the whole thing: "Once consent is received for the passage of convoys through the territory of Republika Srpska, all concerned have to unequivocally observe the regulations involved, and they should abide by these instructions with a view to enriching co-operation with humanitarian organisations and all other protagonists of humanitarian aid in order to enhance the reputation of Republika Srpska at humanitarian level." My question, General: There's so many convoys, and some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina could receive this humanitarian aid only through Serb-held territory. Why -- why is it being repeated time and again that convoys were stopped when a vast majority of them managed to get through?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flow of convoys, as I've already said, was intermittent and not -- did not in any way achieve the targets or goals set by the World Health Organisation. The management of the convoys on the United Nations Protection Force side was done between the UNHCR and the chief of staff of the United Nations Protection Force; first of all, Brigadier General Ramsey, and Brigadier General van Bos [phoen] and Brigadier General Brinkman. They would come and brief me when there were major hold-ups or obstructions taking place. I did not have a detailed knowledge of every single convoy running in Bosnia throughout 1994, and therefore I suggest that your question would be better posed in detail to them, rather than to me, assuming they appear here as witnesses. I can only cover the general position, and that is that, because of obstructions, the delivery of aid did not achieve its targets, particularly at the start of 1994. There were periods when we were able to do so, but there were many periods when we could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apologies. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one particular incident, if it's of any use to you, in, I think, January, when a convoy was blocked coming in from Kiseljak. We summoned NATO air-strikes, and the Serb block withdrew before the NATO air-strikes were used. That was the sort of thing we were having to do to run convoys. On another occasion, we employed Danish Leopard tanks to engage Bosnian Serb tanks in order to facilitate the passage of a convoy bearing refugees from Zvornik. They were extreme examples which I was aware of, but the daily routine running of convoys was not my business. It was the chief of staff of UNPROFOR's business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And thank you. Let me just say this: I'm going to share a statement with you, and then we'll compare percentages. I'm saying that 3 to 5 per cent of convoys, at the most, faced any difficulties, and what would you say? What was the percentage, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a question that is meaningless, because if the United Nations Protection Force was having to employ force or threaten the use of force and was having to deal with obstructive bureaucratic procedures in order to ensure the passage of convoys, then one could not say other than the United Nations was continually facing difficulties. It may have achieved more than 50 per cent of its targets by the time the year ended, but, of course, that includes periods when there was, for example, into Sarajevo, the open running of civilian convoys into Sarajevo during the summer of 1994. And that, of course, distorted the overall tonnages and figures. So if you approached it from a statistical point of view, it is meaningless saying it's this percentage or that percentage. All I know - and this is using World Health Organisation figures - is that because of the obstructions mainly from the Serb side, it was not possible to achieve the targets that had been set for the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, just one more question with this regard. When it comes to the situation in the theatre of war, combats, or cease-fires, did all that have any impact on the passage of the convoys?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, if a high level of conflict was taking place along a certain part of the front-line, then it would not be possible to run convoys across the routes that lay in that part of the line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending -- until the time we get the full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised it is being up-loaded. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I can just add to that, Your Honour. The original of this document is -- because I think the one you see before you has been taken from a book, the original of this document has otherwise been contained at 1D00276, and there is a Defence team translation that's complete of that one. And the translation that was accompanying the one that's on the screen in front of you comes from a book, and, to be quite honest, neither English translation is consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But all the translation will be checked by the CLSS later on. On that basis, we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D690, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D02444 is the next document I would like to bring up. This is a daily report dated 31st January -- or, rather, 30 January 1994, when our co-operation first started, General. And the report was sent after our meeting. 1D0 -- yes, that's it. Can this be zoomed in. I don't believe that we have a Serbian translation: [In English] "I express my gratitude to President Karadzic for his help and co-operation of ensuring unhindered deliveries of humanitarian aid by land corridors passing across this territory. British General Michael Rose -- Major Michael Rose, the newly-appointed UNPROFOR commander ... said after his meeting today with Radovan Karadzic ..." And so on. [Interpretation] But look at the bottom of the page. I am saying my impression is -- [In English] "... that regardless of where they come from, high-ranking officers are the ones least prejudiced. Such was the case with all former UNPROFOR commanders, and so it is with General Rose who is willing to examine the situation as a whole and take an unbiased stand, which the United Nations personifies. We have always been satisfied with the UN high commands and have never had any objections to their works, the Srpska Republika president said." [Interpretation] Here you can see that we -- or that I exculpated higher commands and that we say to the general public that they should be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on several occasions we issued public positive statements about UNPROFOR in order to have common citizens receive them with a lot of understanding and extend welcome to them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember you issuing particular statements, and I certainly cannot remember, looking at that document, expressing satisfaction about the safe passage of convoys across Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the following paragraph, you say -- and let me not read for everybody. Everybody can read it for themselves. You express your satisfaction with the passage of a convoy through the Serbian territory and a lower intensity of military operations or reduced volume of military operations. And it is obvious that you could see a link between the reduced volume of military operations and the increased level -- or, rather, number of the humanitarian convoy passages. That's what you just said a little while ago. If there is a higher intensity of fighting, there are fewer conveys, and vice versa. Do you see the passage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- I can agree that if there's a higher level of conflict, then there would be a lower level of the delivery of humanitarian aid. That's entirely logical. But as I say, I cannot remember ever making a statement expressing satisfaction with the safe passage of convoys, particularly, when I check the table for January, we were running just over half only of the convoys required, so it was most unlikely I would have made a statement of satisfaction. I can't see who else was at the meeting, but had it been a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees present, or even Sergio Viera de Mello who previously worked for the UNHCR, he would certainly have made me withdraw that statement, given the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I'm sure that I didn't write this. And further on, it says that I said that in a discussion with General Rose, we tackled our different issues, some of them being incidents and provocations of Muslim forces with regard to NATO, and that we also agreed that every incident should be investigated. And then on the following page, your words are quoted. Can we go to the following page, to page 2. In quotation, we can see your words: [In English] "'The protection of humanitarian aid routes is within the mandate of the peace forces, and we are aware of the difficulties and traps which can present themselves, but we will conduct an investigation in every case, and I therefore stress the importance of the deliveries of humanitarian aid across these areas,' ..." [Interpretation] You were aware at the time that what was going on was a civil war, and you were aware of all of the difficulties and traps?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said this is a daily report. I take it it is one of the news agencies' report, "Tanjug." Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D691, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D02443 is the next document I would like to call up. 1D02443. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, shall we take a break? We'll have a break for 25 minutes. We'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, General, that the 16 years that have lapsed have had an impact and that we need documents in order to jog our memory of all those events; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly; one's memory starts to fade, and documents are of a help.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the Court to produce P1485, which is Mladic's diary. I would like to ask for English page 90 and the Serbian typed page 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a while ago, General, we saw a "Tanjug" report from our press conference after the meeting. We obviously appeared before the journalists after that meeting, you and I, and here we have your conversation with General Mladic. Can we also see the Serbian typed version, page 91. Not handwritten version, typed version, if that helps. In any case, we can use the English version, and this is what Mladic wrote down. We have both versions now. Mladic says: "I am glad that convoys are going through without problems." This is, according to Mladic, what you said: "We have problems, maybe we will have, but it is best that convoys go. "Life in Sarajevo has been more peaceful in the past seven days." You express your regret, and you say that: "It is regrettable that journalists are attacking only the Serbian side, and the Serbs are not the only ones to blame." In this conversation, reference is made to the convoy, and at that moment you were satisfied with the passage of convoys; right? And the convoys are mentioned both in the conversation with Mladic as well as in the conversation with me that we saw a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember making these comments at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's why we have mementos. This is General Mladic's memento. He said that you had said this. And then you went on to say that: "People in New York think that you are blocking the convoys and UN forces, which is not true." In this case, "you" is actually us, the Serbs. This is apparently what you said to General Mladic on that same day. I understand that a lot has been forgotten. However, it seems to me -- or, rather, I'm even convinced that at that time, you were happier with all that than you are today. Do you agree that both in "Tanjug"'s report about our meeting, as well as in Mladic's notes about your meeting, we can see that you were rather satisfied both with the convoys and the pacification of the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly that was the interpretation you put into whatever remarks you chose to record. Whether that was the case or not, it would be impossible to say today. I would have to get a copy of the record of the meeting that was always kept by the civil adviser of every discussion we had to see whether his notes matched those of yours or General Mladic. But at the moment, it's impossible to say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we get the record made by your civilian administration? Why shouldn't we be able to see for ourselves? But as far as this document is concerned, these are General Mladic's notes, and the previous document was a report from our press conference, after our meeting. I'm not the author of any of them. And this document is self-explanatory. These are your words, both in the newspapers and in Mladic's diary. On the same day, you spoke along the same lines to the both of us; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there's no point of repeating the same question. You made the point, and the general has answered his answer. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to correct the general and say that neither were my notes -- neither the news report nor Mladic's diary. Can this be admitted? I believe that we have to admit parts of Mladic's diary because not the entire document has been admitted. I don't know what the procedure is with the diary parts that we are tendering for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm concerned you have been already exhausted. We admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1P -- or, rather, the same document, English page 109, and the Serbian 110, again the typed version. Page 110 and 111. Let's start with 110. I'm talking about the same document. Can the Court please produce that. This is 15 days later, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of February, a meeting with General Cot and General Rose, and again these are Mladic's notes. He had met up with Generals Cot and Rose. Let's look at the page. A meeting with General Cot, and General Cot says, I've planned a meeting. Can we move on to the following page in the English version as well as in the Serbian version. And he says that he had planned a meeting with General Delic and that he had met Ganic, and he had told me that General Delic was in Central Bosnia, and so on and so forth. And then General Rose is quoted as saying this: "Since we met General Milovanovic, we have had full co-operation." And then he goes -- or, rather, you go on to say: "There's no difference between us and NATO. There will be no air-strikes before I order them." And then you suggest a visit to the weapons collections, and you are asking for guarantees for all weapons to be under control. Do you remember that meeting which was attended by you and General Cot? That meeting was with General Mladic. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the meeting. And I repeat that I have no record in front of me of the meeting taken by the civil adviser, so I can't make any comment as to the accuracy of your account of the meeting. I'm not saying it's inaccurate, I'm merely saying I can't make a comment on it. It's certainly selective in what is written down. It's certainly not comprehensive, your note. For example, it doesn't say that General Mladic flew into a rage and stated that no one can threaten a Serb and live, which is a note that I took from the meeting. That's not included in these notes, so it is selective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you kept any notes from that meeting? Do you have any notes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have notes, but the United Nations certainly kept a record of all the meetings that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll find something about that meeting, sir. 65 ter 318 is the next document I would like the Court to produce. General, in Britain you would also say nobody can threaten Great Britain and remain standing; right? For example, that's what happened at the Falkland Islands, and I congratulate you on that. But I would also say that even small nations have the right, they are entitled to keep their dignity. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which part of the statement you want me to agree with. Nations under the United Nations Charter 7 -- under United Nations Charter Article 7 -- Charter 7, have the right to self-defence. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12318, please. This is not the document that I had called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was this: You said that General Mladic had told you that nobody had the right to threaten the Serbs. Would you not agree that nobody has the right to threaten anybody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. 10785, my mistake, I apologise. 65 ter 10785.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 2. This is a telegram sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan, or, rather, from Ambassador de Mello to Akashi, copied to Annan. Paragraph 2: [In English] "Humanitarian convoys, Rose said, should be allowed to move freely after agreed clearance procedure - including routes - has been complied with." [Interpretation] The first sentence says that a clearance procedure was agreed, agreed clearance procedure, and that it had to be complied with. Further on, it says -- just a moment. Bear with me, please. You can see the entire paragraph, but look at this: "Later with Mladic --" [In English] "-- Rose again expressed satisfaction at the general improvement in terms of convoy movements and hoped this would be maintained. Procedural requirements should not become bureaucratic harassment." [Interpretation] In other words, the procedure did not mean hindrance. [In English] "Serbs must respect you. Not one finger will be raised against the UN. Not one UNPROFOR soldier has died on the Republika Srpska territory. His side had had some problems with members of humanitarian organisations. UNPROFOR convoys would have no problems, other than weather. Some equipment (detectors) could, however, be provided to speed up clearance procedures." [Interpretation] Do you see that even Ambassador de Mello, may God rest his soul, reported exactly in the same way as "Tanjug" reported and in the same way as Mladic had noted it down in his diary?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, elements of what was reported in the first and second documents you showed me are borne out by Mr. de Mello's record of the meeting. And my own memory suggests that Mr. de Mello's record there is accurate, so far as I remember. It's certainly not comprehensive, but it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, General, you will see that Mladic was true to his word. Let's look at 1D02443. We will come back to this document, and we will tender it for admission later. And now I would like the Court to produce 1D02443. Yes, that's the document. Can I draw your attention to the third bullet point, where it says: [In English] "...have arrested three persons for firing on UN aircraft near Sarajevo last week and have issued warrants for the arrest of a further five." [Interpretation] That was in January 1994. There had been an incident, and Serbs arrested and issued warrants for the arrest of others. And look at the last paragraph here: [In English] "The air-lift continues. Three UNPROFOR and 20 UNHCR flights landed at the airport yesterday. Following up last week's incidents of small-arms fire against flights into Sarajevo, the BH -- BSA have arrested three men and have issued warrants for the arrest of a further five." [Interpretation] This is your press release, or, rather, UNPROFOR's daily press release for that particular day. Do you remember this particular incident or --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the country at the time. I took over on the 30th of January, if I remember right, or shortly before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you see that this is consistent with Mladic's position --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very much so. I arrived on the 23rd of January, so I was in the country at the time, but I don't remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with Mladic's position, which was that the United Nations will come in no harm's way, that nobody will as much as raise a finger against them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that certainly seems to be what he said at the time. The fact that the performance on the ground subsequently didn't match up to that promise is an extremely regrettable thing from all perspectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, if we expand this, or if you expand this, we're going to have to seek proof. And we see here that if you don't do anything, the Serbs don't do anything against you, so we see here that it is the perpetrators that are being punished. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's not complete, Your Honour. That's a multi-page document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't mind having all of it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do we have the entire part -- all parts of this document? Do we need to mark it for identification, pending until the time we get all of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D692.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you know that we had offered the doubling of the capacities of land corridors between Belgrade and Tuzla and that we offered that the Banja Luka Airport be opened for humanitarian aid purposes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any particular memory of that proposal or those proposals.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D2535. 1D2535. It's a letter of mine, actually, written to Ambassador Akashi a day after you took up your duties. Here's the letter: [In English] "My meeting with Miss Sadako Ogata on 19th of January, I offered to widen the land corridor for the flow of humanitarian aid from Belgrade to Tuzla, whereby the quantity of aid would be doubled. Not only would aid be expanded but I also promised to facilitate its flow through the proposed Belgrade-Tuzla land corridor. This would accordingly obviate any need for the opening of Tuzla Airport. The Serbian side has legitimate fears that the Muslims wish to smuggle arms through Tuzla Airport, and we are also fearful that they might provoke incidents such as shooting down the aircraft, for which they would blame the Serbs. Ms. Ogata has accepted our offer regarding the expansion of the Belgrade-Tuzla route. Once the peace agreement is concluded, the airport at Tuzla can, of course, be opened, along with several other airports in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Do you agree that this is a fair humanitarian offer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly seems to be an offer which I think Mr. Akashi at the time progressed. Why it never happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll see whether it ever happened. But can this be admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D693, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 6842. 6842 is the 65 ter number. Let us look at the first page and identify what this is all about, and then let's move on to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been admitted as Exhibit P1650.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So much the better. Let's move on to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, let us focus on paragraph 6 "Tuzla Airport." [In English] "Rose commended Karadzic's decision to double quantities of assistance flowing by road, which, if implemented, would reduce the urgency to use the airfield for humanitarian purposes. However, the Secretary-General's letter to the President of the Security Council (which Karadzic had 'read very carefully') made no secret about the imperative need for UNPROFOR to reopen that airport, while taking Bosnian Serb legitimate concerns into account." [Interpretation] This telegram shows that you fully took part in this and that you supported my offer. Now you see paragraph 7. You see this telegram of the UN, dated the 31st of January: [In English] "Karadzic said it would be very difficult for him to agree. He was certain that 'Muslims' intended to shoot down the UN aircraft (he recalled the Italian plane crash, saying, 'They shoot it down and we got the no-fly zone') so as to put the blame on the Serbs." [Interpretation] Do you now remember that you were fully aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're referring to the meeting on the 30th of January, when the subject of the opening of the airfield was raised by Mr. Akashi, and I do remember the discussions which surrounded that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Akashi was there. This seems to have been a meeting between you and me. Actually, do you know these people, Yolanda Auger, who is writing from Zagreb, Lee Trung Zhang [phoen], the civilian chief from Belgrade? Do you know these UN officials?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And I may have conflated a subsequent discussion I had with Mr. Akashi about the opening of the airfield. Certainly, I remember him raising it with you on a subsequent occasion, if it wasn't -- as it looks as though it wasn't on the 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The entire document is most interesting. Since it's been admitted, we can move on. 1D2532, can we have that now, please. It's a letter of mine to His Excellency Mr. Akashi on the 23rd of April, 1994. It relates to the Tuzla airport, and it's also his letter to me on the 21st of March. In the second paragraph, it says: "He demonstrated enormous understanding and flexibility by agreeing that the Tuzla airport be reopened, in the first place, much against our better judgement. However, as in the case of Sarajevo Airport, we decided to accommodate the demands on us in the interests of bringing humanitarian aid to civilians, even though, as you know well, such aid is also being used by the Muslim military and sustains their war efforts against us. I reiterate on this occasion that the modalities of reopening the Tuzla Airport must be in line with the conditions we have agreed with President Yeltsin's emissary." I don't have to read all of it: [In English] "Any forceful scenario for starting the aid flights will, of course, reveal that the international community is not interested in negotiations and agreements, and that the Muslims are dictating to the Serbs side through the UN and others." [Interpretation] So, General, sir, do you not see that we were never opposed to humanitarian aid, even in situations when it exposed us to danger? Our fears were legitimate, weren't they, as stated by the Secretary-General of the UN in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly in a matter -- in the matter of theory, you were not opposed to the delivery of humanitarian aid. But, of course, in practice, as I've explained previously, it was the Serb side that did most of the blocking of the aid convoys. As a matter of point of accuracy, I notice your letter's dated the 23rd of April, but actually there's a time stamp on the letter from the UN Communications Centre which is dated the 23rd of March. I guess your letter should have read "23rd March."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Possibly, because I'm referring to the letter of His Excellency Mr. Akashi, dated the 21st of March. I certainly would not have waited for over a month to reply. I assume that these numbers are more correct, after all. But basically it's one-and-the-same thing. General, since you're saying that, I have to go back to something else. What is the percentage of convoys that did not pass through? But never mind, General. Do you agree with the Secretary-General when he says that our concerns were legitimate? I have to present this to the Trial Chamber. Were we evil, just like that, for no reason whatsoever, or were we cautious, as regards humanitarian aid, so that we would not endanger ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly, you were right to be nervous about the possibility that humanitarian aid could be used to smuggle weapons to the opposing side in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You will see, General, that the Tuzla Airport was widely abused for arming the Muslims. Can this letter be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D694, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D346, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, once again I would like to ask you to take into account the fact that I'm not accusing any nation or any higher command or civilian structure of the UN. However, from this document, you will see proof coming from the Muslim side showing that convoys are being abused. So this is the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without your opposing to his making comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, no, Your Honour. This is at least the fourth document this afternoon that we've received no notification on, so I thought by this time it might be worth rising to make that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
