utterances.text: Yes, I have difficulty following the last three documents from his list of documents to be used with this witness. So what happened, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we had shown it a long time ago. I think that it had been displayed a long time ago. But, nevertheless, we do apologise, we ask for your understanding, because in their statements, witnesses often expand the subject involved and then we have to deal with it. Also, we are very flexible when the Prosecution brings documents out of the blue. This document dates back to the time just prior to your arrival, the 24th of December, 1993. It's the Muslim command and their military security. Could we have page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will tell you to be more cautious when you are going to use the document for which we don't have a translation. You should understand the difficulty of the Prosecution to deal with such matters. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Your Honour, this is a violation of the guide-lines, and it's repeated, and I have particular concern with these multi-page documents in languages that we don't understand, that the witness doesn't understand, where provisions are frequently -- or passages are frequently extracted from those documents and put to witnesses without having the context of the documents explained or properly articulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That noted, why don't we get on with the evidence. So bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The entire document is going to be quite interesting, once we have it translated. But as for this witness, it is only one paragraph that we would like to deal with: "Sector of the Military Security Service of the 1st Corps learned over the past few days that at the PTT building -- PTT engineering building, because of the Christmas holidays, UNPF members have relaxed highly, so they focus very little on their regular tasks." Now, look at this: "In addition to that, because the aggressor has refused to allow logistic convoys for the UNPF into town, there is a considerable shortage of food and oil. Since your oil is not getting in, and that is why the Bosnian Muslim Army doesn't have any oil." See, this is evidence, General. This is proof that we allowed you to import oil for yourselves, and you gave it to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under no circumstances did the United Nations ever give oil to the -- or fuel to the military forces of the Bosnian Government. There was a certain amount of stealing of fuel that took place, and in some cases, regrettably, a number of soldiers individually sold fuel from their lorries to all three sides, depending on who was offering the most money. But it was neither systematic nor deliberate, a matter of policy of the UN, to sell fuel to any side, combat forces. All fuel that was passed across was for humanitarian purposes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this document was shown, I said that I'm not attacking higher commands. But it's all the same, as far as we're concerned, how they got this fuel and how they waged war against us. From our point of view, it's one-and-the-same thing, who sold fuel or whatever, but the fact remains that the more fuel you get into a particular zone, our army is suspicious that that fuel will end up in Muslim tanks or APCs. Can this document please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The quantities of fuel that were stolen from the United Nations or illegally sold by individual soldiers would have been very small and, I suspect, would have more likely gone to civilians rather than the military.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have another opportunity to tender this, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like us to note for the record that the general rejected the possibility of having -- the higher commands have done this, and also he said that it was soldiers at lower levels that sold this. 1D02538 [as interpreted], can we have that, please. 1D02528. The original is in English, so it's going to be easier for us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General -- or, rather, would you agree to have a look at this letter? I wrote to Mr. Akashi on the 24th of June. I thank him for his letter dated the 23rd of June, that is to say, the previous day. And in that letter, he describes the increased difficulties that UNPROFOR BH Command is experiencing with regard to freedom of movement and communication. And then I say: [In English] "Put current methods into some perspective." [Interpretation] Further down, I say: [In English] "I remind you that the recent Geneva Agreement has provided for a cessation of hostilities and exchange of prisoners. The Muslims are completely ignoring their signature over this agreement." [Interpretation] And then a bit further down: [In English] "UNPROFOR forces take little notice of the agreed procedure (for example, undeclared goods and equipment) and display unacceptable behaviour, as if they are an army of occupation. That is even worse -- what is even worse, UNPROFOR is allowing the Muslims to use its observation posts, and there have been many occasions when the blue helmets have used artillery to fire at Serb positions." [Interpretation] Further on, I ask his Excellency, Mr. Akashi, to bring his own influence -- or, rather, to change the manner of action that would actually enhance the Serbs' trust of UNPROFOR. Do you remember this document, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen it before. And I would have taken grave exception to it, had I seen it, and I'm sure that Mr. Akashi would have done the same. There was no case ever of the United Nations allowing its positions to be used by any of the warring parties to prosecute the war, nor, indeed, did the United Nations fire artillery at anybody, other than those people who were trying to obstruct the passage of convoys or in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you did not know absolutely everything that was going on, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that there may have been violations or abuses that you have not been aware of?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the level you suggest in this letter to Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to this sentence: [In English] "But I shall do everything in my power to remove an obstacle to the freedom of movement ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth: [In English] "Equally, as we are in a very delicate phase, I would like you to ask to try to ensure that no unnecessary problems are being created by UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted? And then let's move on to another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, what was your question in respect to the last quotation? I mean, this is a self-serving statement. What was your question to the general?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was whether it was possible that the general, Sir Michael Rose, did not know everything that was referred to in this letter. I am writing to General Rose's boss, because a day before that Mr. Akashi had written to me about difficulties. My question was: Does this letter not show that we have a problem with UNPROFOR? General Rose allowed for the possibility of him not knowing about each and every incident, although he thought that he had to know about major incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That seems to be a complete non-sequitur, and you're far better employed by moving on to something that the general can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You just read out the last paragraph of this document without asking a question to the witness. That's a totally unnecessary waste of time. Let's move on. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thought that that was the question. I thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, did you see that I made efforts to make it easier for UNPROFOR to move about? And you commended me on that note several times, General.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where exactly did I commend you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you'll see. There are quite a few documents in which you expressed your gratitude for my co-operation; for example, this document that we saw a few moments ago, 65 ter 6842. It's a Prosecution exhibit, actually: "In Tuzla Rose commended Karadzic's decision to ..." And so on. [Interpretation] And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was referring to the minutes of the Pale meeting. So why don't we move on? Have we given the number for this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit D695. That's 1D2528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D02471, can we have that, please. 1D02471. It's an UNPROFOR document dated the 8th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think, General, that although you were not aware of this, there wasn't any abuse of UN equipment and insignia by the Muslim Army? This may jog your memory: A few moments ago, you said that you think that that was not the case, but see here, you did know about it. If I have to read it, all right, I will, only part of the first paragraph: [In English] "The BiH have been observed in Sector North-East using UN patches and UN coloured headgear. They have also been observed using white coloured vehicles, and on one occasion, on September 13th, 1994, the vehicle being used was a weapons carrier. This incident was formally protested by Lieutenant General Rose, and photographic evidence was produced for this protest." [Interpretation] This is what you caught, and I'm sure there was a lot of those things that you didn't manage to catch.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're confusing two issues. One was the wearing of uniforms or passing off by the Bosnian Government forces as UN. And certainly, as you observed from that letter, we've noticed this happened from time to time and entered protests. That is not the same as saying that the UN allowed the Bosnian Government forces to use their positions or, indeed, that the UN, themselves, fired their artillery, the inference being that we were fighting on behalf of the Bosnian Government forces. Completely false suggestion. It was an illegal act by the Bosnian Government forces to pass themselves off as the UN, and it stopped whenever we protested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, that was important for you. But for us, it wasn't important who's shooting us if somebody opened fire from a white vehicle and shot our soldier. Mr. Thomas testified here and said that he had to come closer to a distance of three metres to establish that those were not French soldiers, but, rather, Muslim soldiers masked as French soldiers. General, what I'm trying to present to the Trial Chamber is that our concerns and caution were justified; not by the behaviour of higher commands, but by the conduct of soldiers on the enemy side who pretended to be UN soldiers, wearing UN uniforms and patches. Do you appreciate that? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already said once before that I can understand that, as one side or party to the conflict, you wouldn't want these prefaces to happen. That is understood.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, if it is not in evidence already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D696, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce 1D02529.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may remind you, this is my letter dated 22nd June. Obviously, I wrote to Ambassador Akashi on the 22nd of June. He replied on the 23rd, and then I wrote back on the 24th; three days in a row. And you see what I'm writing? "May I draw your attention to a matter of utmost importance, which requires your urgent attention. Over the past few days, Muslim forces in the Tuzla region have been painting over in white many vehicles and giving them UN markings. These vehicles, so painted and marked, have been used for the transport of troops, weapons, ammunition and equipment to the front-lines. Our soldiers on the first lines of defence have clearly observed Muslim soldiers as they got off these vehicles, taking off their weapons and equipment. Thanks only to the maximum restraint exercised by our officers, Serb soldiers have not yet shot at the Muslims operating under UN cover." I don't want to go on reading everything else. And the last sentence: [In English] "If nothing is done, we cannot be held responsible for any mistakes and the consequences thereof." [Interpretation] It didn't happen just once. The Muslim side often resorted to those kinds of behaviour, and approached our lines, or carried out manoeuvres or different actions right before our eyes, and we had to engage in a guessing game as to whether that was them or UN soldiers. Would you agree with me that that was just one of the reasons that made us be more cautious and step up our controls and checks?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask for a reformulation, Your Honour? This is a compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the general can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you know, the procedures were quite clear, Dr. Karadzic, about the movement of convoys. Notification was given 24/48 hours ahead, giving the routes and timings. No other movements took place without that notification, other than myself, for example, that had the need to visit units without warning. But even then, we tried to pass the message if we were crossing on your side. I agree that you had to be careful that the vehicles that you saw painted in white were not the Bosnian Army, who'd camouflaged themselves to look like UN. That is so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One part of the question might have been this: whether this instance had anything to do with tightening the control over convoys at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have not excused the stopping of convoys, the searching of the convoys, because, of course, you knew that -- when we were coming and along which routes we were coming. And, therefore, other movements which were not to do with us, clearly, you had a right to stop and inspect. But as I said earlier, us having gained clearance for the passage of a convoy from you, there was no need after that for you to stop and inspect. And when I say "inspect," I don't mean just asking for the driver for his identity card to make sure he was a genuine United Nations driver; I mean getting in the back of the vehicle and inspecting, at an unnecessary and absurd level, all the items within that vehicle against a manifest which may have been made up, as I say, some 24 or 48 hours before. That it was not compatible and could not be excused by your need to be careful about the passing off, by the Bosnian Government forces, of themselves as UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document will be admitted as Exhibit D697.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you agree with me that the procedure envisaged not only the reading of declarations, but also the inspection, so as to make sure that the declarations matched the contents of the convoys; right? Can you say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I did not think that was compatible with the agreement that had been made that we should have full and free movement across the territories. Notification of the passage of a convoy and the number of vehicles was sufficient, in my estimation. And it was regrettable, as I said already, to me that by the time I arrived, a practice had been embarked upon where parties to the conflict were permitted to go and search vehicles. In my view, and it still remains, that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, all of the documents show that we did not have to trust you; not you, personally, but your soldiers. Declarations were produced to show what was supposed to be in the lorries, and then lorries would be opened to see whether the contents of the lorries matched the declarations. Do you agree that a passage through a country at war allows somebody who has proved something to inspect whether the lorry contained only what was approved and nothing else? Why was that a problem if nothing was being smuggled?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've already answered that question, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you remember where Sepak is and where Karakaj is, both on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Karakaj is close to Zvornik, and Sepak is down the stream. Do you agree that if a license is issued for Sepak, a convoy should not appear at Karakaj, because the crew at Karakaj didn't have a clue that a convoy might be arriving there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without knowing the details, I would agree that a UN humanitarian aid convoy should follow the route that had been agreed previously with the warring parties. That is obvious, from the point of view of security and other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're going to show two more documents about this topic. And do you agree that if a declaration says there would be 10 lorries and 11 appear, that a soldier in charge should not let any of them through until he receives his orders, a new approval for their passage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that seems common sense. But, of course, there are telephones and communications available, and it would not take long to get permission to add one more vehicle to a convoy if that had become necessary. But as I say, I was not responsible for the detailed running of convoys; the chiefs of staff of the UN Protection Force were doing that. And detailed questions of this nature should be directed at them, presuming they appear as witnesses, because I can't make detailed comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the Court please produce 1D00277. We have a draft translation done by my team. Therefore, we have an English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a letter of mine to the MUP of Republika Srpska; in other words, the Ministry of the Interior. We can all see both the Serbian and English versions. The date is 7 August 1994. And in this letter, I issue an order to all MUP organs and all centres of Public and State Security, police stations, check-points, and so on and so forth, which are in direct contact with UNPROFOR and the UNHCR, should try to enhance their relations with those and any other international organisations. And in the following passage, I say that: "Irrespective of frequent cases of abuse and dishonest activities by these organisations, by which they're putting themselves on the side of our enemies, and thus they lose the symbols of neutrality, we must keep improving communications with these organisations ..." And then I say: "When abuses and machinations are detected and corrected according to the rules, and report the cases to the authorise organs of UNPROFOR and UNHCR and organise meetings to shed light on those incidents." General, do you see that we are not actually suspicious of the highest level? What we are saying here is that the higher levels of UNPROFOR and the UNHCR should be notified as to what their soldiers may be engaged in in the field?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the question is should, if you find an infraction in the running of convoys, the UNHCR or the UN Protection Force be informed, well, that is so. In regards to this -- the text of this particular letter, I endorse what you say, in terms of the need to -- at that time to improve the relationships between the two sides, i.e., the UN side and the Bosnian Serb side. I suppose your view, in effect, in regards to this instance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D698, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce 1D2495.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm repeating, General, I'm not accusing anybody, I'm just trying to explain the motives for caution on the Serbian side. This is the long and the short of it. You see that Ambassador Akashi wrote to Annan on the 22nd of July, 1994, about the Iranian flight to Zagreb: [In English] "As you indicate, it is not within our mandate to monitor the arms embargo in the former Yugoslavia. We are, therefore, not in a position to have our personnel inspect these planes to verify that their cargo is of humanitarian goods." [Interpretation] And a bit further down in the second paragraph: [In English] "United Nations military observers at Pleso Airport monitoring the enforcement of the no-fly zone, they have been asked to report if they should observe anything which could indicate a violation of the arms embargo by this flight." [Interpretation] You see, General, sir, that Mr. Annan, Mr. Gharekhan, Mr. Stoltenberg were informed by Mr. Akashi that there was, indeed, correspondence relative to the landing of this Iranian aircraft at Pleso Airport in Zagreb. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly knew there were Iranian aircraft landing at Zagreb Airport. I saw them myself. I was also aware that some correspondence had taken place at the time about this. But I think, as I explained earlier on, we were not in a position to observe whether the embargo was being broken. That was the responsibility of NATO and the European Union, not the United Nations, as Mr. Akashi says in this letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D699, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I remind you that in your book, on page 292, as well as in the statement provided on the 13th of January, 2009, on page 42, you stated that despite the arms embargo, weapons were flowing into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and President Clinton's decision not to impose an embargo on arms gave a new meaning -- or, rather, gave a new sense of urgency to the Serbs. This is your statement, dated 13 January 2009, page 42, paragraph 170, as well as a passage in your book "Fighting For Peace," page 292. At that time, you showed full understanding for us, General; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite see the paragraph you're referring to on page 42 of the hard-back version of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 42 of your statement; page 292 of the book. It's paragraph 170.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 170. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement will be enough, paragraph 170. I may have quoted a wrong page for the book, because I don't know what edition has been taken into account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And your question, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at that time you understood our concerns about the illegal arming of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, of course, we had no knowledge whether the arms embargo was being broken or not. Specific incidents did not get reported to us. There was a suspicion this was happening because, as I explained before, the Bosnian Government forces started to appear in new uniforms. And when General Mladic challenged General Clark, at a meeting in Gornji Vakuf, that the American uniforms were beginning to appear, and no doubt other items of military equipment, General Clark did not deny it. However, as I also have explained, the United Nations' principal job was the delivery of humanitarian aid. We had no intelligence-gathering capability, and so the suspicion remained suspicion. Post facto, of course, 15, 16 years on, it appears that there was an active programme to break that arms embargo by different countries around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, sir, that from Pleso Airport, that armament -- those weapons had to pass through a corridor to the Muslim territory, that some vehicles had to be used to haul those weapons to them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure where you're inferring these weapons are going to. They're going from Zagreb Airport, in your view, to where? To Bihac, or to Sarajevo, or throughout Bosnian Government territory? And, of course, by then Croatia because it was -- a federation had been formed. But I didn't quite get the point of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring -- or, rather, the purpose of my question, General, sir, is to show to this Trial Chamber why we were cautious about the convoys, what caused that caution. It was not any ill will on the Serb side, but the fact that new uniforms, new explosives, new weapons, were arriving, and we didn't know how. We knew that aircraft were landing in Zagreb from Iran and that those weapons were being hauled by convoys, and that was the reason for our concern, and not our ill will against either UNPROFOR or any humanitarian organisations. Do you agree that those weapons had to travel by land and go through certain corridors in order to reach the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly not being transported through the officers or the transports of the United Nations elements deployed. Of course, there was a perfectly good sea route and land route through Croatia. And where the last link occurred, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Time to have a break, Mr. Karadzic, unless you have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said you would come back to the document 10785, which is de Mello's cable to Mr. Akashi. Take a look during the break. We'll have a break for 25 minutes, and we'll resume at 10 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would actually like us to clarify the question of time now. I asked for 30 hours with this witness, who's a participant and a very important one, at that. I got only 10 hours. Even with the best efforts to be made by the Defence, there is no way that we can treat all the subjects that the Prosecution dealt with with this witness, or the documents that are relevant as far as this witness is concerned, so would you please reconsider? I do understand that sometimes I make a comment or two and that I waste a little bit of time that way, but you will see, yourselves, from the transcript that that is minor. If the assertions made by this witness stand, they are conditioned by something else now and they're somewhat different from what they were at the time. Therefore, the Defence cannot believe that they have successfully completed their work here if we do not have enough time to deal with. I believe that we will complete our examination of this witness by Monday, especially if the Prosecution doesn't need too much time. We will make every effort to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I think Dr. Karadzic has made a rather disingenuous characterisation of his cross-examination. It's been filled with argument. Whole documents have been read into evidence, documents that, in fact, sometimes replicate passages of the witness's statement, and I wouldn't think an extension of time would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do you expect your re-examination to be?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this stage, 20 minutes, at the outside, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I confirm with you, just to be correct, the order of witnesses as it stands now? Do we need to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not if we use the KDZ numbers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness will be ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: KDZ369 will be the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the decision, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry I interrupted Ms. Edgerton. Before the decision, if I may, I would like to remind you of all the things we still have to deal with with this witness. It's the total exclusion zone that we have to deal with, then the demilitarised zone at Igman, Bihac, which was brought into the picture against our will, and then we have to finish Gorazde and ethnic cleansing. These are major topics, and we certainly need two days for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was rather -- concerned about the fact whether we have a witness who should testify on specific dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment. Yes, we have one, but he -- and that's KDZ280. But according to the calender, I think he would not be implicated until the week after next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was referring to KDZ310, who was subject to court order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- first of all, I think that's a fair question. I would ask, and I've just sent an e-mail to that effect, to determine whether or not that is, if not technically the case, and I believe in one sense it is, to be the case de facto, and any movement would create a problem. I might add that I had the same concern for other witnesses who -- for whom a similar problem may arise for various other scheduling reasons that were not necessarily brought to the Court's attention by way of specific scheduling, but may have been brought about by virtue of repeated scheduling of that witness or because of the witness's particular circumstances that happened to work out for this particular arrangement, but will be extremely disruptive if altered. So if the Court will give us a moment to check on that, I think we'll be able to provide you with a much more accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is of the view that you should be able to finish your cross-examination by the end of tomorrow. So you will have time, for the purpose of the cross-examination of this witness, until the end of tomorrow. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would like to tender 65 ter 10785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D700.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, Exhibit D700.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for your inconvenience. It is our practice to deal with the matters related to the witness in the absence of the witness. During your absence, we told the accused to finish his cross-examination by the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I ask for document 1D00278 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, General, I would like to put something to you, or, rather, to the Trial Chamber, first and foremost, our efforts for the humanitarian aid and everything else to flow unhindered, without us suffering any kind of damage, military damage, that is, and without having the other side gain an advantage. Or, actually, would you agree that if warring parties agree to something, not a single one of these warring parties should gain any advantage from that kind of agreement? What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a hypothetical question. I'd have to have a specific case that you would quote that I could refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I meant whether it was legitimate to make sure that the other side does not gain an advantage on the basis of the goodwill expressed by the first side. If you couldn't glean that much, let's deal with the document. This is my letter from the 17th of August. Do you remember that in August there was that letter of mine about improvement of relations with UNPROFOR, and a few other letters? And now we see the 17th of August. This is an order of mine. It is being sent to Professor Koljevic, as the person chairing the body for co-operation, also to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the Co-ordination Committee for Humanitarian Aid. Do you agree that this document is being sent to the aforementioned persons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the first order: "Convoys and official personnel of humanitarian organisations may move in the territory of Republika Srpska only with authorisation of the Co-ordination Committee of the Government for Humanitarian Relief of Republika Srpska. "The head of the State Committee for Co-operation with UNPROFOR shall pass a regulation for a method of issuing permits for the movement of convoys and officials of international humanitarian organisations in the territory of Republika Srpska." Do you agree that this is a rather high level? The vice-president of the republic heads the team that is supposed to co-ordinate co-operation with you with regard to humanitarian issues?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that Mr. Koljevic was the person on the Bosnian Serb side with whom we dealt on the passage of convoys. That is so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the second page in Serbian. For the time being, the English is all right. It's the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 in Serbian and in English: "From the check-point, according to the estimate of the authorised public safety official, to the place of unloading or passing to a territory of other parts of the former BiH, the convoy shall be escorted by a police patrol." It should say "patrol," actually. That's the word that should be used, "patrol," rather than "escort." So all humanitarian activities in the territory of Republika Srpska should be carried out in accordance with International Humanitarian Law. Do you agree, General, that, as you had put it yourself, I had 1.600 kilometres of a front-line?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we discussed that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that I was very busy with political negotiations with the entire international community?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you know Serbs well enough, you will agree that it's very hard to reach concord among Serbs within the country among 60 municipalities so that everything can work properly. In spite of all this hard work, would you agree that the highest authorities of Republika Srpska are making every effort to improve co-operation with UNPROFOR, especially with regard to humanitarian issues? Regardless of the results, to the best of your knowledge, were efforts being made?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have to set your question in context, Dr. Karadzic. At the start of my period in Bosnia, the flow of aid, as we've seen from my comments, was clearly not too bad. Following the agreement to withdraw heavy weapons from around Sarajevo, which took place at the beginning of February, the flow of aid improved immensely across Bosnian Serb territory, until the attack was launched into Gorazde and the subsequent air-strikes that took place as a result of that attack. There was then a complete halting of all the aid. Fortunately, we were able, through discussion, to restore that aid, and between April and September of that year the flow of aid continued more or less unblocked, certainly into Sarajevo, although it still remained difficult to get aid through to Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, although that did occur from time to time. We had enforced the passage of a convoy to Maglaj another enclave, and the convoys in and out of Bihac remained patchy, but did flow. Following the attack by the Bosnian Government forces against the Bosnian Serb side in Sarajevo in the middle or towards the end of September, then the aid flow started to be interrupted by the Bosnian Serb side, and it wasn't until January of that next year that we came to a final agreement on the passage of -- uninterrupted passage of aid into Sarajevo, in particular. So the situation came and went with regard to the flow of humanitarian aid. The end result of all our efforts to deliver aid to the people who needed it in Bosnia, as I say, never -- rarely met the objectives of the World Health Organisation. That is the general picture which you can set in context any period of time you like, and you will see whether the aid was flowing at that particular moment in time or not. In August, there was quite good flow of aid, particularly after the sniper agreement, I seem to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, if you remember, it was your very own estimate that that period had a significant decline in the number of casualties as well; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a considerable reduction in the number of casualties in the war in Bosnia throughout 1994, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, General, that in a conflict, there are two parties, and that both should agree to have peace established, or, rather, that the behaviour of one side considerably depends on the behaviour of the other side too?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inevitably so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D701, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, you stated these are dealt with by the chiefs of staff, but can you see the para 1? Para 1 says --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be coming. Para 1 seems to refer to two entities, one being the Co-ordination Committee of the Government for Humanitarian Relief, the other being State Committee for Co-operation with UNPROFOR. Do you remember such entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir. I mean, maybe the chiefs of staff knew the distinction, but I certainly did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D02453. 1D02453. Yes, we have it in English. I believe we don't have it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a document --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think this document should be broadcast. Could I just have your indulgence for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was just looking at the provider, Your Honour. Your indulgence, please. Until I'm certain, and out of an abundance of caution, do you think we could possibly deal with this document in private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What we are seeing now in Serbian seems to be a document originating from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the previous document. This is the previous document. It's the Serbian version. The other document was removed from the screen. I am sorry, there is no reference to Rule 70, and that's why I simply asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we shall go into private session, Ms. Edgerton, or is it safe, unless we are broadcasting this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised we can go without broadcasting this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I leave it in your hands because I'm not aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just been confirmed to me it's definitely a document we should deal with in private session, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D02527.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As we can see, this is my letter to His Excellency Mr. Akashi on the 5th of September, in response to his letter of the 3rd of September. He mentions parts of some speech of mine out of context, and then I say: [In English] "We do not, at present, intend to impose any sanctions against the Muslims. A decision to introduce such sanctions, moreover, would not affect normal humanitarian aid provided that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is not blocking humanitarian aid destined for the Republic of Srpska." [Interpretation] And then further down: [In English] "Since Yugoslavia is imposing economic sanctions against us, we feel entitled to continue commercial sanctions against Muslims. As you know, however, this policy does not cover gas, water, and electricity supplies to the Muslims. You are, of course, aware that the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo is openly delighted at the recent turn of events in the relations between Yugoslavia and the Republic of Srpska. This being the case, they should not complain if, given the genocidal sanctions against us, we impose some limited sanctions on them. I am sure, Excellency, that you can see our point of view?" [Interpretation] Do you agree, General, that we were under sanctions imposed by the entire world, and from the 4th of August onwards, under sanctions imposed by Yugoslavia as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some vague knowledge that sanctions had been imposed, but I was focused on what was happening in Bosnia, not outside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do recall that those sanctions were imposed upon us to force us to accept the contact group plan; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't be able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we can see, both from the previous document and from this document, that we make a distinction between commercial convoys that may be subject to sanctions, although we had not decided to do that, and humanitarian convoys that are not subject to any sanctions; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears so from your letter to Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D703, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce 1D0245 [as interpreted]. 02459, 1D02459. This is a summary of a meeting with me at Pale on the 19th of August, 1994. And in the first paragraph, we can read: [In English] "Together with DFC General Crabbe, HCA de Mello, General Rose, CAC Andreev and others, I held a meeting with Dr. Karadzic in Pale at 12.30. Also present from the Serb side were Generals Mladic and Tolimir, Koljevic, Krajisnik and Buha."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that, or do you have anything about that in your notes, or do you still recollect that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect it, but I can remind myself by reading the letter or the document on the screen and the extract from my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If needed -- actually, we will go swiftly through the document. You can see, for example, in paragraph 4, that Karadzic completely agreed with the necessity of a diplomatic alternative with regard to the contact group plan. And then, paragraph 6, with regards to relations with UNPROFOR, Dr. Karadzic said that the Serb side fully appreciated the United Nations efforts, although their presence had saved the Muslims from complete defeat. [In English] "The Serb objective was, he said, to separate the societies in which -- in B and H, much like had happened in Scandinavia in 1905, and between India and Pakistan following World War II. While it was the intention of his side to become 'good neighbours' and while the Bosnian Serbs ..." [Interpretation] Next page: [In English] "... were not planning to take any new territory ..." [Interpretation] And so on. And further on we talk about the total exclusion zone. Can we go one page ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the general asked for an opportunity to review the document and the excerpt from his book. I just wonder why he shouldn't be allowed to have that opportunity, rather than to have us hear passages of this document read into the record again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, have you done with the second page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read them all now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to see the third page? I think it's a four-page document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is exactly what I wanted us to do, to go swiftly through the document. And if the general needs to take some time to read the document -- it says here: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic further stated that the roads had not been closed to humanitarian aid --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you don't have to read that. Let us know when you've done with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've done with it -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. What is your question? What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that occasion I stated that humanitarian convoys, as it says here, were not closed, that all that was closed were opportunities for the black market to thrive and for weapons to be brought in? Perhaps you can see that sentence, and do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the sentence. Which one is it? Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Third line from --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third line from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be the third line from the bottom of paragraph 11, would it? That's the one I've got on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third line from the very top of the page. The sentence starts with: "Dr. Karadzic further stated ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember and do you agree that our position was that the only restrictions applied to the black market and weapons, and that we subscribed to anything else?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time the humanitarian aid convoys were flowing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at bullet point E in the 12th paragraph. Can we scroll up the page a little. Would you please look at bullet point E, and everybody can read for themselves, so as to prevent me from reading it aloud. This is about human rights in Banja Luka/Bijeljina, and it says here that: "Dr. Karadzic shared your concerns over the abuse of human rights and that the authorities were trying to control extremists in those areas. In Bijeljina, the authorities intended to soon replace the chief of police as the level of security he was providing to the population was unsatisfactory." I also said that Bijeljina was the 'Hong Kong' of the Serb republic, and so on and so forth. "In some cases, some residents had voluntarily asked to leave for Tuzla, and on arriving in Tuzla, had claimed that they had been expelled." [Interpretation] Do you remember, General, sir, when it came to refugees, that refugees enjoyed one kind of benefits and social contributions, and when people voluntarily crossed over, they did not enjoy those same benefits?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the United Nations distinguished between refugees and voluntary refugees, if that's how you would describe them. People who were in need were in need. Whatever their antecedence were didn't concern the United Nations. And as you'll remember, the United Nations Protection Force had no representatives in Banja Luka or in the neighbouring regions, and these reports came from UNHCR observations, not from the protection force.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the very bottom of that page were some other concerns of ours mentioned: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic's response was that while UNPROFOR was welcome to stay, the international community's attempt to scare them with threats of its withdrawal would not work, stating that, 'We would not object to your departure. We would divide Bosnia into two with the Croats, and there would be no Muslim state' ..." [Interpretation] There's a threat of ours. And then it goes on to say: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic asked if this was what the international community really wanted. He said that while the Muslim people were for peace, their leaders were not, and if their offensives continued, the Serbs would launch a counter-offensive 'and humiliate them.' Both Karadzic and Mladic warned against UNPROFOR leaving weapons for the Bosnian side if it withdrew. I told them that we had no intention of doing this, and disassociated the force from remarks made by certain troop-contributing nations, i.e., Malaysia, in this vein." [Interpretation] Do you remember that some battalions [Realtime transcript read in error "Italians"] coming from some contributing nations did not behave fairly and that they expressed their friendship by helping the Muslim side, by even giving them weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge, and I refute the allegation that the -- any United Nations element was giving weapons to the Bosnian Government forces. I think you're referring in this -- or Mr. Akashi is referring in this to an unfortunate statement made by one of the Malaysian press offices, for which I think he was duly reprimanded, but I don't remember the detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To be clear: General, is this the document authored by Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's a document authored by Mr. Akashi, but I'd have to scroll back to the start, sir, to see that. But it certainly would have been the result of him asking his secretary to put this memorandum together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D704.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, in paragraph 142 of the general's statement, he refers to a meeting on this date involving Mr. Akashi, Mr. de Mello, General Crabbe and himself, so I would think that the general's conclusion is entirely accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And line 21 of page 84 should refer to "internationals" instead of "Italians." That could be checked out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The word was "battalions," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Has this been given a number? Can the Court please produce 65 ter 11048.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, sir -- I checked, and indeed the chief of police in Bijeljina had been removed. Do you remember that I orally reported to you about that because the level of security was not satisfactory in Bijeljina, people did not feel safe there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I had no knowledge of what was happening in an area where we didn't have any United Nations representation from the Protection Force side, so I can't make comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we have another telegram sent by Ambassador Akashi to Annan, Gharekhan and Stoltenberg in Geneva. If we have agreed on that, can we now go to page 3. This is a report on a meeting between General Lapresle and Ambassador Akashi with me at Pale. Let's look at paragraph 10: [In English] "In response to my request that the ICRC be allowed to evacuate Muslims from Prijedor, Dr. Karadzic said that the situation in Prijedor was an unfortunate development for the Serbs. While he accepted that the situation could have been predicted (he noted that civilians in the town had, at the beginning of the war, slaughtered each other), he maintained that the present situation had been prompted by a Muslim massacre of six Serb policemen from the town. Currently, additional forces had been sent to the town to stabilise the situation, and he had initially agreed to the ICRC request to evacuate individuals who feared for their lives, based on the belief that the numbers concerned were minimum. However ..." [Interpretation] Next page: [In English] "... the ICRC --" next page, please: "... had indicated they intended to evacuate 80 truckloads of people at one go and this was unacceptable. He had no objection to them evacuating up to five trucks of people a day (approximately 100 people), as this would allow those left behind to reconsider their situation in light of the stabilised conditions in the town." [Interpretation] Therefore, do you remember, General, sir, that at that time the International Red Cross put a lot of pressure on me, and you can see that they even resorted -- or, rather, they asked General Lapresle and Akashi -- they put a lot of pressure on me to allow them to take people from Banja Luka and Prijedor to third countries, and here a reference is made to Prijedor, although I believe that that should not be done? And if, indeed, that had to be done, it had to be done gradually so as to show people that there was no reason at all for them to leave?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't party to that discussion and have no record of it. And as I've already said, we didn't have people deployed on that side of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I respect that, General, sir. But you did say after 1994, and especially after the Markale incident and other such incidents, the Serbs had stepped up their ethnic cleansing in Bosnian Krajina. However, my thesis is this: The International Red Cross had invested a lot of effort to take away a huge number of Muslims and Croats from that same Krajina, whereas I, myself, was greatly opposed to that. I have a lot of evidence to prove that, and one piece of evidence is this meeting between General Lapresle and Akashi with me. What I'm trying to do is establish whether you were misinformed, whether you thought that that evacuation actually -- what was an evacuation was about ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would have to point out where I allegedly said that after the bombing in the market-place, the Serbs had stopped their ethnic cleansing in Bosnian Krajina, because, of course, that was not within my area of responsibility. And as regards the rest of your comment, I can't make a comment because, as I've said, I was not party to that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was just an off remark in the examination-in-chief, but it may be detrimental to the Defence, and that's why we have to deal with the issue. Could you please look at paragraph 12 and see what it says there: [In English] "Turning them to the issue of ethnic cleansing and the violation of human rights in Banja Luka and the need to halt this practice, I suggested that I visit the area towards the end of next week. I further requested the UNPROFOR --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the point, Mr. Karadzic, of going further, after having heard from the witness here, that he's not aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that the document will jog the general's memory, because both Lapresle and -- as the chief commander, and Akashi, as the civilian chief, tried to look at the situation and deploy UN troops in Banja Luka. But one thing is certain, and I'm sure that General Rose is familiar with that, if we move on to paragraph 16, which is on the following page -- I'm moving through the document very slowly, and you will see that there is a reason for that. In paragraph 16, please. You see that General De Lapresle briefed Karadzic about the use of close air support to defend UNPROFOR troops under attack, and requested the VRS Army co-operation, ensuring that there were no actions that could lead to its use: "Dr. Karadzic said that the VRS had no intention of attacking UNPROFOR troops and that the unfortunate incident surrounding the Maglaj convoy was an aberration and that that would be dealt with." And now, sir, you see here: [In English] "I emphasise the distinction between close air support as an act of self-defence and air-strikes as an offensive or punitive action." [Interpretation] This was something that I wanted to present to the witness when we were talking about the attacks primarily against Gorazde and later on when the general had already left, and it was then explained to me that close air support was something that was a defence mechanism, something to defend UNPROFOR troops, and we always gave you the right to shoot if you were attacked; whereas, by contrast, air-strikes are punitive and offensive measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was clearly the view of the author of this document, but certainly it wasn't my view. And I think I explained it, at a technical level, the difference. The subject of close air support or the expression "close air support" covers the general support which ground troops can expect from the air. Air-strikes are a specific use. The offensive or defensive element in that technical analysis is not there. It could be used either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, on the 7th of April, Mr. Akashi informed me that there was a difference, and you know that Mladic always said, If our troops attack you, shoot, nobody will hold it against you. Mr. Akashi, in the presence of General De Lapresle, said that close air support was, as it says here, self-defence and that air-strikes are an offensive or punitive measure. Did you call for a close air support or air-strikes in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've explained to you, the presence of the NATO aircraft over Bosnia was in the nature of close air support. I certainly called air-strikes on the tanks and artillery that were attacking Gorazde. Now, you can decide whether that was defensive or offensive. In my book, it was a defensive action taken under the United Nations Security Council Resolution 824 and 836.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But General, sir, you did not come under attack in Gorazde. It was two forces that were fighting in Gorazde, and NATO put itself on one side. That was the Serb perception, that NATO sided with one of those two warring parties. Can we go to the following page: [In English] "In terms of punitive and offensive action --" [Interpretation] Please, paragraph 20: [In English] "On Gorazde, he expressed concern that the reports of the UNMOs in the pocket did not tally with the Presidency reports of mass destruction and killing and requested clarification on this discrepancy. He also said that it was time for the Security Council to take more decisive action on the opening of Tuzla Airport for humanitarian flights." [Interpretation] That was part of that meeting with Izetbegovic. Do you see how the situation developed? And we're talking about the 7th of April here.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember reasonably well how the situation developed because, of course, that was the time at which we were having to deal with the Bosnian Serb side to try and deter them from attacking any further into the enclave of Gorazde. At the same time, we were having to reassure the Bosnian Government side, in particular Mr. Silajdzic and President Izetbegovic, that the casualties rates which they were describing were nowhere near the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make one submission in this regard. This is a document that could very easily have been dealt with by way of written motion. It's of that category of document. But we've spent some time now with the general repeatedly having to affirm that he can't comment on this document, rather than actually get to the point. It seems to me there could be a more efficient way of spending the time that we have here, but we have no objection to the document going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D705.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document about that same topic. I believe we have time, a short passage. 65 ter 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was about to say that I agree with Ms. Edgerton's observation. And in such circumstances, you can't complain about shortage of time. Bear that in mind. We have only two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 8025. With all due respect, Your Excellency, we have a problem with the general's memory. I would like to jog the general's memory about what he said during his chief examination, and the difference between that and what he wrote in his documents at the time, and I can't do it in writing. The Trial Chamber will then have an opportunity to contrast the two and maybe render a decision at my detriment, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is the 11th of April, 1994, sent to the president of Republika Srpska, the chief of staff, and so on and so forth, and that was sent by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, signed by Manojlo Milovanovic. Can we please see the third page of the same document, the paragraph that concerns Gorazde. Page 3, Article A, bullet point 2 "The Herzegovina Corps." Bullet point E: "Throughout the day in the general area of Gorazde, the NATO air forces carried out a reconnaissance and engaged in provocations by launching mock attacks on VRS units. Between 1500 hours and 1545 hours, while the Muslim forces were conducting a synchronised attack on the left bank of the River Drina, the enemy attacked units of the Herzegovina Corps, killing three (one officer - physician) and nine wounded soldiers. Two medical vehicles, one PAT," and so on and so forth, "were destroyed." Do you agree, General, sir, that the Serbian perception of this co-operation between NATO aviation and the Muslim infantry must have looked terrifying?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no co-operation at all between the Bosnian Government forces and NATO, and any interpretation on your side that that was the case was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the Muslim infantry exploited the effects of NATO air-strikes. They launched simultaneous attacks while we were being stricken by the NATO aviation, while our facilities were being pounded. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that a question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like the general to -- I'm not saying that the United Nations had anything to do with that. It was NATO that attacked us, and the Muslim side exploited the results of that attack and launched their infantry attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's what I'm asking you, General, sir. I'm not saying that that was the case. I'm not saying that you approved that or not. I am saying that the Muslims benefitted from the NATO punitive expedition.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well have been so, but it certainly wasn't the result of any co-ordination between NATO and the Bosnian Government forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1662, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, once you've heard the answer from the witness, just move on to your next question without making any statements. We'll resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
